questions.questionText: What does owning a single share of a company give you?

answers.text: A loan to the company
A fractional ownership stake in that company
Guaranteed dividends every year
The right to vote on every business decision

questions.explanationText: A share represents part-ownership of a company. Shareholders own a slice of the business proportional to how many shares they hold.

questions.questionText: What is an IPO?

answers.text: An internal price offer between existing shareholders
When a private company first sells shares to the public
A government bond issued to the public
A type of dividend payment

questions.explanationText: IPO stands for Initial Public Offering — the first time a private company offers its shares for purchase on a public stock exchange.

questions.questionText: What is a dividend?

answers.text: A fee charged when you sell shares
A penalty for holding shares too long
A portion of company profits paid to shareholders
The difference between buy and sell price

questions.explanationText: Dividends are distributions of a company's profits to its shareholders. Not all companies pay dividends — many reinvest profits back into the business.

questions.questionText: A company has 1 000 shares outstanding, each worth 100 NOK. What is its market capitalisation?

answers.text: 1 000 NOK
100 NOK

questions.explanationText: Market capitalisation = share price × number of shares outstanding. Here: 100 NOK × 1 000 = 100 000 NOK.

questions.questionText: Which entity sets the day-to-day strategy of a public company?

answers.text: The shareholders directly
The stock exchange
The company's management team
The government regulator

questions.explanationText: Shareholders elect a board of directors, who in turn appoint management. Day-to-day decisions are made by the management team — shareholders vote on major decisions at annual meetings.

questions.questionText: What happens to a stock's price when there are more buyers than sellers?

answers.text: The price falls
The price stays the same
The price rises
Trading is suspended

questions.explanationText: Stock prices are driven by supply and demand. When demand (buyers) exceeds supply (sellers), buyers must offer higher prices to attract sellers — pushing the price up.

questions.questionText: Which single factor most strongly drives a company's long-term share price?

answers.text: The company's social media following
The company's earnings (profits)
The number of employees
The age of the company

questions.explanationText: Over the long term, a company's earnings growth is the primary driver of its share price. In the short term, sentiment and news play a larger role, but profits ultimately determine value.

questions.questionText: What does 'volatility' describe in the context of a stock?

answers.text: How frequently a stock pays dividends
How many people own the stock
How quickly you can sell the stock
How much the price swings up and down over time

questions.explanationText: Volatility measures the degree of price variation over time. A highly volatile stock can move sharply in either direction, indicating higher risk and potential reward.

questions.questionText: A company reports earnings far below analyst expectations. What typically happens to its share price?

answers.text: It rises because the company is honest
Nothing — only dividends affect the price
It falls as investors sell in disappointment
The stock is automatically delisted

questions.explanationText: Markets react strongly to earnings surprises. When results miss expectations, investors often sell, pushing the price lower — even if the company is still profitable.

questions.questionText: What is 'market sentiment'?

answers.text: The total value of all stocks on an exchange
A government report on economic conditions
The overall mood (optimism or pessimism) of investors collectively
The average dividend yield of the market

questions.explanationText: Market sentiment refers to the overall attitude of investors toward a market or asset. Positive sentiment (bulls) drives prices up; negative sentiment (bears) drives them down.

questions.questionText: Which statement best describes the risk-return relationship in investing?

answers.text: Lower risk always leads to higher returns
Risk and return are unrelated
Higher potential returns typically come with higher risk
Government bonds always outperform stocks

questions.explanationText: The risk-return trade-off is a fundamental principle: to earn higher potential returns, investors must accept higher risk. There is no free lunch in investing.

questions.questionText: Which type of risk can you reduce by investing in many different companies?

answers.text: Market (systematic) risk
Inflation risk
Interest rate risk
Company-specific (unsystematic) risk

questions.explanationText: Diversification reduces unsystematic (company-specific) risk. If one company fails, others in your portfolio can offset the loss. Systematic risk affects the whole market and cannot be diversified away.

questions.questionText: What is 'liquidity risk'?

answers.text: The risk that a company runs out of cash
The risk that you cannot sell an investment quickly at a fair price
The risk that inflation erodes your returns
The risk of currency fluctuations

questions.explanationText: Liquidity risk is the danger of being unable to sell an asset quickly without accepting a significant price discount. Small-cap stocks and real estate often carry higher liquidity risk than large-cap shares.

questions.questionText: Even a savings account carries some risk. Which risk is it?

answers.text: Default risk — the bank might go bankrupt
Volatility risk — the balance fluctuates daily
Inflation risk — rising costs erode the real value of savings
Liquidity risk — you cannot withdraw your money

questions.explanationText: Inflation risk means the purchasing power of your money decreases over time. If inflation is 3% and your savings account pays 1%, you are effectively losing 2% of real value per year.

questions.questionText: A stock whose price varies by 20% annually is described as having higher __ compared to a stock varying by 4%?

answers.text: Liquidity
Yield
Volatility
Dividend coverage

questions.explanationText: Volatility is measured as the standard deviation of returns. A stock swinging 20% per year is far more volatile than one swinging 4%, meaning it carries more short-term price risk.

questions.questionText: What does a bondholder receive that a shareholder does not automatically get?

answers.text: Voting rights at company meetings
A share of company profits
Fixed interest payments (coupons) and return of principal
Ownership of the company's assets

questions.explanationText: Bonds are debt instruments — the bondholder lends money and receives scheduled interest (coupon) payments and the principal back at maturity. Shareholders own equity and receive no guaranteed payments.

questions.questionText: In a company bankruptcy, who gets paid first?

answers.text: Common shareholders
Bondholders (creditors)
Preferred shareholders
All are paid equally

questions.explanationText: In liquidation, creditors (including bondholders) have a higher claim on assets than shareholders. Common shareholders are last in line and often receive nothing.

questions.questionText: Which asset class typically offers higher long-term returns but with more short-term volatility?

answers.text: Government bonds
Corporate bonds
Stocks
Both are identical in risk and return

questions.explanationText: Historically, stocks have delivered higher long-term returns than bonds, but with considerably more year-to-year price swings. Bonds offer more stability but lower expected returns.

questions.questionText: When interest rates rise, what typically happens to the price of existing bonds?

answers.text: Bond prices rise
Bond prices fall
Bond prices are unaffected
Bond coupon payments increase

questions.explanationText: There is an inverse relationship between interest rates and bond prices. When new bonds offer higher coupons (due to rising rates), older lower-coupon bonds become less attractive and fall in price.

questions.questionText: Why might an investor include both stocks and bonds in their portfolio?

answers.text: Bonds amplify stock returns
Stocks and bonds often move in opposite directions, reducing overall risk
It is a legal requirement
To maximise tax liability

questions.explanationText: Diversifying across asset classes — stocks for growth potential, bonds for income and stability — can smooth out a portfolio's returns over time, as they often respond differently to economic conditions.

questions.questionText: What is 'compound interest'?

answers.text: Interest calculated only on the original principal
Interest earned on both the principal and previously earned interest
A fixed interest payment regardless of balance
Interest charged for withdrawing money early

questions.explanationText: Compound interest means you earn returns on your returns. Over time, this causes your investment to grow exponentially rather than linearly — it is the 'eighth wonder of the world' according to many investors.

questions.questionText: You invest 1 000 NOK at 10% annual return. Approximately how much will you have after 10 years with compounding?

answers.text: 2 000 NOK
1 100 NOK
2 594 NOK
5 000 NOK

questions.explanationText: With compound growth, 1 000 NOK × 1.10^10 ≈ 2 594 NOK. Simple interest would only give 2 000 NOK. The extra 594 NOK is the power of compounding.

questions.questionText: Why does starting to invest early make such a large difference?

answers.text: Early investors pay lower fees
Stock markets only grow when young investors participate
More time allows compounding to multiply returns over a longer period
Early investors receive government subsidies

questions.explanationText: Time is the most powerful ingredient in compounding. Each additional year multiplies your total return. Starting 10 years earlier can more than double your final portfolio value.

questions.questionText: What is the 'Rule of 72'?

answers.text: You must diversify into at least 72 stocks
Divide 72 by the annual return to estimate how many years to double your money
You should invest 72% of your salary
A stock index rebalances every 72 days

questions.explanationText: The Rule of 72 is a quick mental maths shortcut: 72 ÷ annual return % = approximate years to double. At 8% return, 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years to double your investment.

questions.questionText: Which of the following benefits most from compound interest over a long period?

answers.text: A savings account with monthly withdrawals
A stock portfolio where dividends are reinvested and left to grow
A fixed-term deposit with annual withdrawals of interest
Cash kept under a mattress

questions.explanationText: Reinvesting dividends and letting them compound is the textbook example of compounding in action. Each reinvested dividend buys more shares, which in turn pay more dividends.

questions.questionText: What is the primary purpose of diversification?

answers.text: To guarantee positive returns
To reduce the impact of any single investment performing poorly
To increase the overall risk of a portfolio
To concentrate on the best-performing sector

questions.explanationText: Diversification spreads risk across multiple assets so that a poor performance by one does not devastate the whole portfolio. It does not eliminate risk, but it reduces unnecessary concentration.

questions.questionText: An investor holds only shares in one oil company. Which risk are they most exposed to?

answers.text: Inflation risk
Currency risk
Company-specific (unsystematic) risk
Liquidity risk

questions.explanationText: Concentrating in a single company means any bad news specific to that company — a scandal, poor earnings, or management failure — hits your entire portfolio.

questions.questionText: Which type of risk CANNOT be eliminated through diversification?

answers.text: Company-specific risk
Industry-specific risk
Systematic (market) risk
Management risk

questions.explanationText: Systematic risk (market risk) affects all investments — a global recession, for example, hits virtually every asset class. Diversification reduces unsystematic risk but cannot remove systematic risk.

questions.questionText: A well-diversified portfolio might include which combination?

answers.text: Only technology stocks from one country
Stocks, bonds, and assets from multiple sectors and regions
Only the ten largest companies in one index
Cash and gold only

questions.explanationText: True diversification spans asset classes (stocks, bonds, real estate), sectors (technology, healthcare, energy), and geographies (domestic, international, emerging markets).

questions.questionText: What is 'correlation' in the context of portfolio diversification?

answers.text: The fee charged to manage a diversified fund
A measure of how similarly two assets move in price
The number of assets in a portfolio
The annual return of a portfolio

questions.explanationText: Correlation measures how closely two assets move together. Low or negative correlation between assets means they tend to move differently, which is the key to effective diversification.

questions.questionText: On a candlestick chart, what does the body of a candle represent?

answers.text: The highest and lowest prices of the day
The difference between opening and closing price
The trading volume for the day
The dividend paid that day

questions.explanationText: The body of a candlestick shows the range between the opening and closing price. A green/white body means the close was higher than the open (bullish); red/black means the opposite (bearish).

questions.questionText: What does a 'moving average' show on a stock chart?

answers.text: The average trading volume over a period
The smoothed average price over a defined number of days
The predicted future price
The total return including dividends

questions.explanationText: A moving average smooths out day-to-day price fluctuations to show the underlying trend. A 50-day moving average, for example, shows the average closing price over the past 50 trading days.

questions.questionText: What does high trading volume during a price increase generally suggest?

answers.text: The price rise is likely to reverse soon
The move has weak conviction behind it
Many investors support the move, giving it stronger conviction
The stock is about to be delisted

questions.explanationText: Volume confirms price moves. A price rise on high volume suggests broad market participation and conviction. A rise on low volume may be less reliable and more likely to reverse.

questions.questionText: What is a 'support level' on a price chart?

answers.text: The highest price a stock has ever reached
A price level where the stock tends to find buying interest and stop falling
The average analyst price target
The price at which the company buys back its own shares

questions.explanationText: A support level is a price zone where demand has historically been strong enough to prevent further decline. Traders watch these levels as potential entry points or as warning signs if they are broken.

questions.questionText: What does the term 'trend' mean in technical analysis?

answers.text: A sudden one-day price spike
The general direction in which a price is moving over time
A stock that is popular on social media
A guaranteed future price direction

questions.explanationText: A trend describes the general price direction over time: uptrend (higher highs and higher lows), downtrend (lower highs and lower lows), or sideways. Technical analysts look for trends to guide trading decisions.

questions.questionText: What does an index fund aim to do?

answers.text: Beat the market through active stock picking
Invest only in government bonds
Replicate the performance of a specific market index
Invest only in dividend-paying stocks

questions.explanationText: An index fund passively tracks a market index (e.g., S&P 500, Oslo Børs All-Share) by holding all or a representative sample of the index's securities in the same weights.

questions.questionText: Why are index funds generally cheaper than actively managed funds?

answers.text: They invest in fewer companies
They require no fund manager to pick stocks, so costs are lower
They are only sold to professional investors
They are sponsored by governments

questions.explanationText: Active funds pay managers to research and select stocks, increasing costs. Index funds follow a rules-based approach requiring minimal human intervention, resulting in much lower annual fees (expense ratios).

questions.questionText: What is an ETF (Exchange-Traded Fund)?

answers.text: A bond that pays interest monthly
An index fund that trades on a stock exchange like a share
A government savings scheme
A fund that only invests in emerging markets

questions.explanationText: An ETF is a type of index fund that is listed and traded on a stock exchange, just like individual shares. This gives investors flexibility to buy and sell throughout the trading day at market prices.

questions.questionText: Studies show that over long periods, most actively managed funds:

answers.text: Consistently outperform index funds after fees
Match index funds exactly
Underperform index funds after fees
Are guaranteed to deliver positive returns

questions.explanationText: Academic research consistently shows that the majority of actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index after accounting for fees over long periods. This is a core argument for passive index investing.

questions.questionText: What does it mean that an index fund provides 'instant diversification'?

answers.text: You receive your money back instantly
The fund splits your investment across all companies in the index in one purchase
All your money is converted to foreign currency
You are protected from all losses

questions.explanationText: Buying a single index fund share gives you exposure to all the companies within that index. For example, a global index fund might spread your investment across thousands of companies worldwide.

questions.questionText: What is dollar-cost averaging (DCA)?

answers.text: Investing a lump sum at the lowest price of the year
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals regardless of price
Converting all savings to US dollars
Selling shares whenever the price averages out to your purchase price

questions.explanationText: DCA means investing a consistent amount (e.g., 500 NOK per month) on a regular schedule. This automatically buys more shares when prices are low and fewer when prices are high.

questions.questionText: What is the main benefit of DCA during a falling market?

answers.text: You stop buying, protecting you from losses
You automatically buy more shares at lower prices
You receive a government bonus for continued investing
Your existing shares increase in value

questions.explanationText: When prices fall, your fixed investment amount buys more shares. This lowers your average cost per share over time — a process called 'averaging down' — so you benefit more when prices recover.

questions.questionText: Which psychological benefit does DCA offer?

answers.text: It guarantees you buy at the absolute lowest price
It removes the need to time the market, reducing emotional decision-making
It eliminates all investment risk
It doubles your return compared to lump-sum investing

questions.explanationText: One of DCA's greatest advantages is removing the temptation to time the market. By investing automatically on schedule, investors avoid making fear-driven or greed-driven decisions.

questions.questionText: An investor uses DCA and buys 3 months in a row at prices of 100, 50, and 100 NOK per share. What is their average cost per share?

answers.text: 75 NOK
100 NOK
50 NOK

questions.explanationText: With a fixed monthly investment (say 100 NOK): Month 1 = 1 share at 100, Month 2 = 2 shares at 50, Month 3 = 1 share at 100. Total: 4 shares for 300 NOK → average 75 NOK per share. Lower than the simple average of 83.33.

questions.questionText: In what scenario might a lump-sum investment outperform DCA?

answers.text: When markets are volatile
When markets consistently rise throughout the investment period
When interest rates are rising
When you are investing for less than one month

questions.explanationText: If markets rise steadily, a lump-sum investment deployed immediately captures more of the gains. DCA is most advantageous in volatile or declining markets. Over the long run, both strategies tend to produce similar results.

questions.questionText: What is paper trading?

answers.text: Trading shares printed on physical paper certificates
Simulated investing with virtual money to practise without real risk
A government-regulated trading test for new investors
Trading only in paper and publishing companies

questions.explanationText: Paper trading is the practice of simulating buy and sell decisions without using real money. It lets beginners learn market mechanics, test strategies, and build confidence before risking actual capital.

questions.questionText: What is a key limitation of paper trading compared to real investing?

answers.text: You cannot track your performance in paper trading
Paper trading does not simulate the emotional pressure of real money on the line
Paper trading always shows worse results than real trading
Paper trading uses outdated price data

questions.explanationText: The biggest gap between paper and real trading is psychology. Knowing you can 'reset' removes the fear and greed that profoundly affect real trading decisions — skills developed in paper trading may not fully transfer.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a good use of paper trading?

answers.text: Generating actual income from the stock market
Testing a new investment strategy before committing real money
Guaranteed practice that will make you profitable in real markets
Replacing real investing entirely for the long term

questions.explanationText: Paper trading is excellent for testing strategies, understanding order types, and learning how markets work — all without financial risk. It is a stepping stone, not a substitute for real investing.

questions.questionText: If a paper trader consistently profits in simulation, what should they conclude?

answers.text: Their strategy will definitely work with real money
Their strategy shows promise, but real trading will test it more rigorously
They should immediately invest all their savings
Paper profits equal real profits

questions.explanationText: Paper trading success is promising but not guaranteed to translate. Real trading involves emotions, slippage, transaction costs, and taxes that simulation often cannot perfectly replicate.

questions.questionText: Which concept does paper trading help you practice that is crucial in real investing?

answers.text: Filing tax returns on investment gains
Applying for a brokerage account
Entering and exiting positions according to a plan, not impulse
Receiving dividends from companies

questions.explanationText: Discipline — sticking to your strategy and not reacting emotionally to short-term price moves — is one of the most important investing skills. Paper trading helps you build and test this discipline in a safe environment.
